body.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon murder trial exposed dangerous pattern of controlling behaviour
The double murder trial of Beau Lamarre-Condon not only exposed him as a callous killer, but also revealed him to be a controlling man who stalked and "petrified" a former partner.

Former NSW Police officer Lamarre-Condon shot dead Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police pistol in Mr Baird's Paddington home on February 19, 2024, before disposing of their bodies in rural Bungonia, south of Sydney.
Lamarre-Condon was on Wednesday found guilty of two counts of murder and one count of aggravated break, enter and steal.
It took the jury about two hours to return unanimous verdicts.
In the lead-up to the murders, Lamarre-Condon had exhibited a dangerous pattern of behaviour amid his "jealous infatuation" with Mr Baird, after their brief casual relationship.
The double murderer monitored Mr Baird's subsequent relationships, interfered with his social media accounts, reviewed Snapchat locations, stalked him and broke into his home.
When Mr Baird firmly reiterated the end of their casual fling to Lamarre-Condon, the former officer's obsessive conduct escalated.
Lamarre-Condon did not take no for an answer.
'They were the real deal'
Mr Baird, 26, was a television presenter who grew up in Melbourne and loved AFL.
In one obituary, a friend wrote: "[Jesse's] effervescent personality was infectious."
Friend and former colleague Isaac Muller had told 774 ABC Melbourne: "Jesse was a very spontaneous and adventurous soul … he was just so free and loving."
Mr Davies, 29, grew up in Queensland, was an international flight attendant and loved camping and travel.
A friend and colleague of Mr Davies wrote on social media: "He was not just a close friend; he was a source of inspiration, a constant reminder of the beauty in life."
When Mr Baird met Mr Davies on New Year's Eve in 2023, they quickly formed a close connection and made things official in early 2024.
"There was something about Luke that just lit Jesse up," one friend of Mr Baird told the court during the trial.
"They were the real deal."
Mr Baird's mother described Mr Davies and her son as completely "smitten" with each other.
The prosecution said Lamarre-Condon was aware of the new relationship.
Mr Baird discussed the situation with his former long-term partner, Corey-Dean Thorpe, who gave evidence Mr Baird sounded "petrified" and was worried about Lamarre-Condon's access to a gun.
Mr Baird's sister, Kourtnee Baird, told the trial she noticed her brother was fearful, scared, shaken up, and suspected Lamarre-Condon was following him.
Queer community's pain
The murders of Mr Baird and Mr Davies sparked outrage across Australia, especially among the queer community.
"Being a Brisbane boy, Luke was someone who was known to and dearly loved by many people in my own circles," Ben Bjarnesen, founder of the LGBTQ Domestic Violence Awareness Foundation, said.
"We had attended parties and community events together, so the news was particularly close to home."
Following the murders, Mr Bjarnesen attended the Sydney vigil for Mr Baird and Mr Davies in the lead-up to Mardi Gras.
"There was an overwhelming sense of grief, but also hurt, anger and disbelief," he said.
The NSW Police commissioner at the time, Karen Webb, initially delayed speaking publicly about the case and then described it as a "crime of passion".

When later pressed on that decision, she responded with a reference to the lyrics of pop song Shake It Off, by saying: "There will always be haters. Haters gonna hate — isn't that what Taylor Swift says?"
Ms Webb later clarified her "crime of passion" description, saying her intention had been to distinguish the motive from a gay hate crime and describe it as a crime of a "domestic nature".
For domestic violence advocates, however, the language used was a painful misstep, given the term minimised the seriousness of domestic violence-related murder.
Controlling behaviours in gay relationships
About three in five LGBTQIA+ people in Australia have experienced intimate partner violence in their lifetime, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

"LGBTQIA+ community members tell us that it is difficult to get the support they need and that they experience discrimination from services that are supposed to help," ACON's chief executive Michael Woodhouse said.
"Our communities still feel pressure to prove our relationships are valid. That can mean people don't seek the help they need from services or law enforcement."
The behaviours leading up to the murders — stalking, surveillance and violating boundaries — can feel common in gay dating and relationships.

The Sorting It Out report, published in 2019 by Western Sydney University in collaboration with ACON, found young gay, bisexual, queer and trans men were more likely to accept certain controlling behaviours within relationships.
These behaviours included reading a partner's emails or texts without his permission, putting a hand around a partner's throat, and dictating who a partner could and could not be friends with.
Mr Bjarnesen said the behaviours were not always recognised for what they were; forms of domestic violence and coercive control.

"Behaviours like monitoring someone's movements, checking their phone, excessive messaging, stalking, jealousy and repeatedly violating boundaries can become normalised or even mistaken for signs of love, care or commitment," he said.
Mr Bjarnesen's work has been shaped by his own experience of domestic violence in a same-sex relationship.
"During my own abusive relationship, I experienced many of these behaviours … I didn't recognise them as domestic violence,"
he said.
He called for government campaigns, mainstream media and support service advertising to make sure LGBTQIA+ victim-survivors were not left out of the conversation.
Now, the bereaved loved ones of Mr Baird and Mr Davies await the perpetrator's sentencing hearing in March.
"What was so evident that evening at the Sydney vigil was just how deeply loved they both were and how profoundly their deaths had affected the community," Mr Bjarnesen said.
